prompt.context: Our client is a for-profit, specialty college named Chic Cosmetology University (CCU). Founded in 2005, CCU is a program for high school graduates seeking their professional cosmetology license. CCU is currently the market leader for cosmetology education with campuses in ten major metropolitan areas in the US.
prompt.question: CCU has capital to invest in a new campus and is considering Chicagoland as a location. Should they do it? The client considers a successful launch as achieving positive operating profit for the new campus two years after opening.

clarifying_info.q: What are CCU's revenues and costs?
What is the cost to open a new campus?
clarifying_info.a: The total cost is $4.5M in initial building costs to renovate its chosen site. These costs can be amortized evenly over a three-year period. Fixed costs remain flat per year.

CCU has identified 1,000 targeted high schools in the Chicagoland area. Within these high schools, CCU's market research estimates that on average 6 students per high school have potential for CCU enrollment. 80% of enrolled students come directly from high school; the other 20% come from the adult market.
There are 2-3 other large specialty colleges, some of which are in the same geographies as CCU. Community colleges are beginning to offer cosmetology degrees at lower prices.

clarifying_info.q: How long have CCU and competitor campuses been operating?
clarifying_info.a: All ten CCU campuses have been present for at least three full school years. All competitor campuses have also been present for similar lengths of time.
A high school diploma and cosmetology degree are required to enter the field. 98% of cosmetologists are women. CCU and industry enrollments are growing at 5% per year.
CCU boasts the best campuses in the industry with state-of-the-art equipment and strong job placement due to relationships with top salons in local areas.

exhibits.title: 2010 CCU Financials
exhibits.shows: A financial summary table for all CCU campuses as of 8/31/2010, showing student enrollments, revenue, fixed costs broken into subcategories, variable costs broken into subcategories, and operating profit. All figures are in thousands of dollars.

exhibits.title: CCU and major competitor campus locations
exhibits.shows: A map of the US showing CCU campus locations (marked with one symbol) and major competitor campus locations (marked with another symbol), alongside a table of each CCU campus city and its 2010 market share of total potential students as defined by CCU.

data.note: Share measured as share of total potential students as defined by CCU

framework: 1. Understand CCU's revenue and cost structure (revenue per student, fixed costs per campus, variable costs per student, gross profit per student)
2. Determine break-even enrollment for the Chicago campus, incorporating both ongoing fixed costs and amortized build-out investment
3. Estimate the total addressable market in Chicago (potential HS students + adult market)
4. Project CCU's likely market share in Chicago based on competitive dynamics
5. Estimate year 1 and year 2 enrollments and compare to break-even
6. Identify qualitative risks and strategic alternatives

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate: (a) average revenue per enrollment, (b) total annual fixed cost per campus, (c) total variable cost per student, and (d) gross profit per student.
questions.guidance: Candidate should divide systemwide figures by 10 campuses or 10,000 students to derive per-unit economics.

math.setup: Revenue per enrollment = Total revenue / Total enrollments; Fixed cost per campus = Total fixed costs / 10 campuses; Variable cost per student = Total variable costs / Total enrollments; Gross profit per student = Revenue per enrollment - Variable cost per student
math.answer: Revenue per student: $15K; Fixed cost per campus: $4.8M; Variable cost per student: $8K; Gross profit per student: $7K

questions.prompt: What is the break-even number of students required for the Chicago campus in year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate must add yearly amortization of the $4.5M build-out cost (spread over 3 years = $1.5M/year) to the base fixed cost, then divide total fixed costs by gross profit per student.

math.setup: Total annual fixed costs (Chicago) = Base fixed cost per campus + Annual amortization; Break-even enrollments = Total annual fixed costs / Gross profit per student

questions.prompt: What types of high schools and students does CCU target in Chicagoland? How large is the potential student market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should think through targeting criteria before being given the specific numbers. After noting plausible criteria (public schools, middle-class areas, geographically close, female HS graduates not attending 4-year college), the interviewer shares the market data. Candidate then calculates total potential students including the adult segment.

math.setup: Potential HS students = students per HS x number of targeted HS; Potential adult students = HS potential x adult ratio; Total potential = HS + Adult
steps: Potential HS students = 6 students/HS x 1,000 HS = 6,000 students
Adult market = 20% of total enrolled base implies adult potential = 6,000 x 25% = 1,500 students (since 80% HS means adult is 20%, and 6,000 / 0.8 x 0.2 = 1,500)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what market share should CCU expect in Chicago, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that campuses without competitors achieve ~14-16% share while campuses with one competitor achieve ~10-12% share. Boston (8%) is an anomaly. Chicago has one competitor, so 10% is the reasonable assumption. A strong candidate will also flag that the 10% figure is for mature campuses (3+ years) and Chicago is unlikely to reach that share in year 1 or year 2.

math.answer: 10% market share assumption for Chicago (one competitor present)

questions.prompt: How many students should CCU Chicago expect to enroll in year 1 and year 2? Does it break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate multiplies total potential students by the projected market share, then applies 5% growth for year 2, and compares to the 900-student break-even.

math.setup: Year 1 enrollments = Total potential students x market share; Year 2 enrollments = Year 1 x (1 + growth rate)
steps: Break-even is 900 students; Year 1 shortfall = 900 - 750 = 150 students; Year 2 shortfall = 900 - 788 = 112 students
Chicago does NOT break even in year 1 or year 2 under current assumptions
math.answer: 750 students in year 1 (150 short of break-even); 788 in year 2 (still 112 short). CCU does not achieve positive operating profit within two years.

questions.prompt: (Bonus) Suppose CCU finds a lot with a one-time construction cost of $300K (same 3-year amortization). Should they enter Chicago now?
questions.guidance: Candidate recalculates break-even with lower amortization. However, an excellent candidate recognizes that the 10% market share benchmark applies to campuses present for 3+ years — Chicago is a new market and will not achieve that share in years 1-2, so even a lower cost structure does not make entry feasible under the 2-year profitability target.

math.setup: New annual amortization = $300K / 3 = $100K; New total fixed costs = $4.8M + $0.1M = $4.9M; New break-even = $4.9M / $7K
steps: Year 1 estimate = 750 students > 700 break-even — numerically it works
However: the 10% share is for mature campuses; a new campus is unlikely to hit 10% in year 1 or 2, so 750 is an optimistic ceiling, not a reliable forecast
math.answer: Numerically break-even falls to 700 (below 750 projected), but the projection is based on mature-campus market share data and therefore overstates realistic year 1 enrollments for a new campus. Entry remains inadvisable.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative issues and strategic alternatives should CCU consider?

categories.name: Demand generation
ideas: Offer scholarships to increase the number of potential students and/or improve conversion rate
Strengthen high school outreach and recruiting in targeted Chicagoland schools
Leverage CCU's salon placement network to market careers to prospective students

categories.name: Alternative markets
ideas: Consider other cities that currently have no CCU presence where competition is absent and share could reach 15%
Evaluate adding a second campus in high-share cities like NYC or Atlanta where capacity may be constrained
Perform market research in other cities to identify higher potential-per-HS ratios

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce fixed costs by transporting equipment and materials from campuses that are not at full capacity
Negotiate a lower-cost renovation site to reduce the initial build-out below $4.5M
Explore shared services across campuses to lower recruiting, general, and administrative costs

categories.name: Pricing and positioning
ideas: Differentiate further on placement outcomes to justify premium pricing and sustain the $15K revenue per student
Evaluate whether a slightly lower tuition could meaningfully increase enrollment volume and overall profit

categories.name: Market share ramp
ideas: Recognize that new campus market share typically ramps over 3+ years; model a phased break-even timeline beyond year 2
Invest in brand-building ahead of launch to accelerate share ramp in Chicago

recommendation: CCU should NOT enter the Chicago market under the current cost structure. Even at an optimistic 10% market share, the Chicago campus would enroll only 750 students in year 1 — 150 fewer than the 900 required to break even. Year 2 enrollments of approximately 788 also fall short. The client's two-year profitability target cannot be met.
risks: The 10% market share assumption is based on mature campuses (3+ years of operation); a new Chicago campus will likely achieve less in years 1-2, making the enrollment shortfall even larger
Community colleges entering with lower prices could further compress CCU's addressable market
Upfront $4.5M capital outlay is at risk if enrollment targets are not met
next_steps: Identify alternative cities with no current CCU presence where market share could reach 14-16%
Explore ways to reduce the Chicago build-out cost significantly (e.g., the $300K lot scenario lowers break-even to 700, but only if realistic year-1 market share can be achieved)
Commission market research in Chicago to test whether potential-per-HS exceeds the 6-student average assumed here
Model a longer (3-year) break-even horizon if the two-year target is relaxed
